chunks: And by this same chain of narrators: from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Ibn Bukayr, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh (peace be upon him),
who said: 'There is no objection to urinating in flowing water.'
All these reports collectively indicate that flowing water bears no legal ruling of ritual impurity whatsoever. Then he said — may Allah the Exalted support him —:

Istinja' is not required of the one purifying from the hadath of sleep or passing wind; rather, that is required only of the one who has defecated. This is indicated by the fact that legal obligations (al-dhimmam) are originally free of any rulings attached to them, and we do not attach any ruling to them except what is definitively established by a shar'i proof. And there is nothing in the shari'ah that indicates the obligation of istinja' from sleep and passing wind. This too serves as an indication thereof.

key_terms.اسْتِنْجَاءٌ: istinja' — ritual cleansing of the private parts after excretion
key_terms.الذِّمَمَ: al-dhimmam (pl. of dhimma) — legal obligations borne by a person; the principle here is their original freedom from rulings
key_terms.النَّجَاسَةِ: najasah — ritual impurity; a legal category of filth requiring purification
key_terms.حَدَثِ: hadath — a state of ritual impurity requiring wudu or ghusl

ai.seo_question: Is istinja' obligatory after the hadath of sleep or passing wind according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This entry from Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām transmits a ruling of Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (AS) — via Ḥammād, Ḥarīz, and Ibn Bukayr — that there is no legal objection to urinating in flowing water, from which the author infers that flowing water bears no juridical ruling of ritual impurity. The cited jurist then applies the foundational principle of original freedom from obligation (barāʾat al-dhimma) to rule that istinjaʾ is not obligatory after the ḥadath of sleep or passing wind, being required only after defecation.
